archetype.name: Lottery Team (out-shot)
archetype.definition: A club that is losing the puck and the shot battle so badly that only its goaltending keeps games close, and whose record reflects genuine play rather than bad bounces.

report.headline: Woll is keeping it respectable, but the Flyers are being buried in shots.
report.take:
Ten games in, Philadelphia sits last in the Metropolitan and 29th of 32 on the site. The record looks like a hard-luck start: eight straight losses, three of them in overtime, several by a single goal. The underlying numbers say it is not bad luck. The Flyers own 34% of the 5-on-5 expected goals and 41% of the shot attempts, and both are last in the league. They get 21.2 shots on goal a game and allow 32.8, the second-fewest and the most. Both roster groups grade F. No skater is carrying a line: the top six forwards by ice time all sit between roughly 28% and 37% xGF.

The goaltending is the reason this has not been a rout. Goalies GSAx is 4.1, 7th in the league, and nearly all of it belongs to Joseph Woll (.916, 4.3 GSAx). Dan Vladar has been below expected at .889. Under that much volume, the defense still ranks only 20th in goals against, which is a credit to the crease rather than the system. The penalty kill (83.8%, 10th) helps too.

The offense is where noise and signal overlap. A 6.6% shooting rate against a league norm of 11.3% will not hold, and the 96 PDO says the bounces have run cold. More finishing would turn some of those one-goal and overtime losses into points. The volume problem underneath is structural, though. Few shots, a 31st-ranked power play at 10.3%, and the league's worst offense mean even normal shooting luck only lifts this to a below-average attack. Matvei Michkov (4 goals, 41st among right wings) and Porter Martone (the best xGF on the top lines at .44) are the bright spots.

This also breaks from recent history. Last season's 98-point club and the two before it all posted xGF shares above 50%, so a 34% share is a collapse, not a continuation. Ten games is a small sample and some of it will snap back toward the club's norms. Even so, the roster grades and the shot gap point to a team playing for the draft lottery, not for a playoff spot.

strengths.title: Woll is stealing goals
strengths.body: Joseph Woll has stopped more than four goals beyond expectation in his five starts, which is why the team GSAx ranks 7th despite the league's heaviest shot load. That kind of number is volatile over a short sample. A goalie seeing this many shots is also more exposed to a cold week. He deserves the bulk of the starts.

strengths.title: A penalty kill that holds
strengths.body: At 83.8%, the PK is 10th and well above the league's 79%. Combined with the goaltending, it keeps games within a goal. It is also above what Philadelphia managed the last two seasons, so a small sample is likely flattering it.

strengths.title: Shooting luck owed back
strengths.body: Skaters are converting 6.6% of their shots, last in the league, and PDO sits at 96. Finishing at that level is not a skill a roster sustains, so goals should come a little easier. With so few shots, though, the payoff is modest.

concerns.title: Last in every possession measure
concerns.body: The Flyers have the league's worst xGF % and CF %, and they allow the most shots on goal a game. This is the core of the season, not a quirk of the schedule. It is also a sharp drop from the 50%-plus expected-goal shares of the last three years. Some recovery is likely, but an F-graded forward group and blueline cap how far it goes.

concerns.title: The offense barely exists
concerns.body: At 1.55 goals a game the Flyers rank last. The power play converts 10.3%, roughly half the league rate, and the shot volume is 31st. The listed defensemen have one goal combined, so offense from the back end is almost nonexistent.

concerns.title: Blueline underwater across the board
concerns.body: Jamie Drysdale is logging 22 minutes a night with a .296 xGF and a -4.1 Game Score. Cam York's .266 in his five games is even worse. Travis Sanheim plays over 25 minutes at -9. When the top-minute defensemen are this outplayed, the shot gap is no surprise.

trend.note: After a nine-game skid, the Flyers have taken points in three of their last five, including back-to-back wins over Ottawa and Colorado. Goals against in that stretch are down 0.87 a game from the season rate. The improvement is mostly goaltending and a few more finishes, not a turnaround in the shot share.

weekAhead.headline: Three beatable opponents, but each exposes the shot gap differently
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in Buffalo and finishes with two home games against Anaheim and Columbus. None of the three ranks in the site's top half; Buffalo is 26th and Columbus 27th. On paper this is a chance to build on the two wins. Buffalo and Columbus both have leaky penalty kills, and Buffalo's goaltending has been among the league's worst.

The catch is that Philadelphia is out-shot by nearly everyone. Buffalo controls 54% of shot attempts, 7th in the league. Anaheim allows only 21.7 shots a game, so a low-volume Flyers attack may struggle to find the net at all. A split-plus week is realistic if Woll stays hot. Expecting a sweep would be reading the opponents' records rather than the matchups.

keyMatchups.title: Buffalo's porous net and penalty kill
keyMatchups.body: The Sabres stop 86.1% of shots, 30th, and kill only 64.5% of penalties. Their defense has also allowed forwards the most points above expectation in the league. If the Flyers' shooting luck is ever going to turn, this is the game. The risk is Buffalo's puck control piling up shots on Woll.

keyMatchups.title: Anaheim's power play vs. the PK
keyMatchups.body: The Ducks convert 26.9% on the power play, 6th in the league. That tests a Philadelphia kill that has been one of its few strengths. They also allow the third-fewest shots, which is bad news for an offense already 31st in shot volume.

keyMatchups.title: Columbus: a division game to win
keyMatchups.body: The Blue Jackets are 29th on the PK at 68%, rank 26th on offense and sit 27th on the site. It is a home game against a division rival only a couple of wins ahead. The Flyers' 31st-ranked power play has to cash in when Columbus gives it chances.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Flyers can push their shot total into the mid-20s against Buffalo and Columbus; until that happens, every win leans on Woll.

restOfSeason.body:
The current pace (41 standings points over 82 games) is too bleak. Shooting at 6.6% will climb, and the possession numbers are so far below this franchise's recent seasons that some return toward the mid-40s in xGF share is likely. The opposite pressure comes from the goaltending: Woll's start is the best-case version of him, and Vladar has been below average. Some of the goals saved now will be given back. My estimate is a final total around 66 to 80 standings points. That is a clear step back from last season's 98 and well out of the playoff race, with scoring rising to roughly 2.4 to 2.8 goals a game the rest of the way.

What would change that view is the shot share. If the 34% xGF is a ten-game collapse rather than a new level, this roster has shown it can play near even. If it holds even around 40%, the lottery is the realistic destination, and the season becomes about Michkov, Martone and the young defensemen.
swingFactors: Whether the 5-on-5 shot share recovers toward recent seasons' levels
Woll sustaining above-expected goaltending under heavy volume
A power play that has converted barely half the league rate

confidence.note: Ten games is a tiny sample, though the shot-share gap is extreme enough to take seriously.
